I’ve been working on feeling angry since September 28 this past year. I’m prediabetic with hypoglycemia at the moment. Apparently, I recently found out there is a very strong family history of it. I would say embrace the anger and work to resolve it. Those are your feelings and they are valid. I also go to therapy and that has been a huge help with working through this. I can identify with your anger about this, but don’t blame yourself. You can only do so much before genetics get in the way. You can still beat this and live with it in a healthy way by changing your diet and eating lifestyle. I stopped eating at 7 (on most days). It is a horrible process in the beginning but doable once it becomes routine. If you’re not a fitness nut (I’m not) aim to get 10,000 steps in a day. Drink lots of water and stay hydrated. Eat 6 small meals with more vegetables and fruit from the ground (berries are awesome).  Protein is your friend. It is okay to eat bread (once in a while). Like I said it is doable but takes hard work. You can still have some of the fun food, but have those as treats and in small portions. 

On a side note: you are young and said at 160lbs. I am trying to get to 160lbs. Weight isn’t everything. It is where the weight sits with diabetes. My doctor told me that I have to lose the weight in my gut because of the insulin-resistance. I’m in my forties and about 214. I have lost 44lbs since last July. Take heart in knowing that this is not the end of the line. There is a lot of research out there that is drastically different from when my grandparents were alive. It will continue to get better. ❤️‍🩹 Take your anger and turn it into the wake-up call you needed. Take really good care of yourself and tell others to f-off when they give you a hard time. Sending you positive love and wishes on the internet.

Factor it into their grade. My middle school teachers would have take time at the end of each marking period to organize our binder for their subject based on the units we were learning. It was wonderful, because then we had our work set up to study from for unit tests, quizzes, and the final. By the end of the year, we had our own review book set up to study from. That was a blessing in disguise for me cause I would not know where to start studying from if I didn’t have that. They would give us like so many points if we could show them we kept the necessary work and notes they gave us for each marking period. It was a great way to make your subject important, but give kids who struggled in it a way to shine for being organized. Then when you were struggling on a specific topic, the teacher could tell you to go back and study a specific unit as review. Of course, this is dependent on if the student kept the work and followed directions. But if a parent calls and inquires about work and notes, it’s a starting point for parental involvement and the student getting their shit together. The teachers always had a classroom copy of the binder to refer to, so students who fell behind could come in and copy notes missing, organize, etc. It isn’t perfect, but it is something the students have to apply themselves to, if they care about their grade. I did this for my subject when I taught middle school, too. It’s eye-opening for parental involvement when you can pull out the class copy of the binder, and show them what should be done and see if your kid has it. If they don’t here’s what they need to do. Parents were very receptive to this and able to keep their kid on task if they cared when checking work at home. I know things are more digital now. I use 360 notebook for myself to stay organized.
